utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Case IT-01-47-T, the Prosecution versus General Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have the appearances. Prosecution first, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, the case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter, Mathias Neuner will be joining us shortly, and sitting in with us today, Mr. President, is the Chief of Prosecutions, Mr. Gavin Ruxton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. May we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, myself, counsel; and Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. For the Defence of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, the legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber would like to say good morning to all those present, the representatives of the Prosecution, and we'd like to take advantage of this occasion to greet the Chief of Prosecutions, who is here and sitting next to Mr. Mundis. We'd also like to greet the Defence counsel and the accused and all the staff in the courtroom, the court reporters and the interpreters, who are outside the courtroom but nevertheless with us, and the security staff. We're going to continue today with the hearing devoted to the videotapes, but I was given to understand that Mr. Mundis would like to take the floor first before we go ahead, so Mr. Mundis has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I've asked to briefly address Your Honours and the Defence with respect to ongoing progress concerning the issues raised in the Trial Chamber's oral order of 17 May 2004. We have completed several of the additional tasks which the Trial Chamber directed us to do. I would ask at this time, Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher, to distribute some documents. These documents, Mr. President, contain known and original signatures of the two accused. There are photocopies of the documents available and then two folders, which I understand the Trial Chamber wished to view, containing the original signatures. Once those are distributed, I will briefly explain what the material that's being passed out is, and there are sufficient copies for the Defence, the accused, the Trial Chamber, and the legal officer. Perhaps the usher could provide the two coloured folders to the Trial Chamber. Mr. President and Your Honours, you will note the photocopied documents are -- contain actually three different documents. There are sets for both of the two accused. The first document, the page that's in B/C/S, is the arrest warrant and order for the surrender of the accused. At the time that the two accused surrendered, they signed the bottom of the arrest warrant and order for surrender. The original of those documents is in the blue folders. The second page in the photocopied set is an information sheet which the accused fill out at the time of their surrender in this case, which also contains the handwriting of the accused. The original, again, is in the folders. And finally, with respect to each of the two accused, Mr. President, there is a Rule 68 disclosure certificate. At the request of the Rule 70 provider, the accused were personally required to sign for this material. Unfortunately, I am not in a position to disclose precisely what this material is; however, you will notice that both the accused and their counsel signed for receipt of this Rule 70 material and that was disclosed under Rule 68. And again, you have the original of those receipts attached to the front of the arrest packages. If there are any questions about that material, I'm happy to address them. Otherwise, I'll move on to the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're providing us with a binder with folders and the originals bearing the signature of the accused, one of the accused, the arrest warrant, and the other document with the signature, which will allow us to verify and see that the photocopies with the signatures do in fact correspond to the original signatures. So there were two sets. We have two sets here for each of the accused, with the signatures. With the exception of General Kubura's file, the arrest warrant -- no. No, there is his signature here. It said "copy," but in fact it's the original. So we do have what we need for the two accused, their signatures. Would the Defence counsel like to take a look at the files? They are original documents. You have them. Fine. Please continue, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would simply ask if in fact these documents are going to be in any way appended to the record as any kind of Court exhibits or any similar thing, that they be placed under seal, particularly with respect to the Rule 68/Rule 70 document, which is a very sensitive document. We would ask that if in fact this is made part of the record, that these two documents with the signatures be placed under seal. Mr. President, as you're aware, Ms. Benjamin is currently in Sarajevo. Let me take this opportunity to briefly inform you as to the status of future witnesses. The witness Judge Adamovic, as I indicated earlier, will be available the week of 21 June. As of yesterday, there was at least one and perhaps two of the archivists that Ms. Benjamin has spoken to are also available that week. It is at this point our intention to schedule the archivists and Judge Adamovic for the week of the 21st of June, with a sufficient number of witnesses to fully engage our work efforts during that week. Of course, once we have any additional statements from Mr. Adamovic or any statements from the archivists, those will be disclosed as quickly as possible. My understanding is that Ms. Benjamin has taken those statements in both English and B/C/S so as to avoid the need to have the documents translated once she arrives back here in The Hague and so that the witnesses could sign the documents in their own language, which should expedite matters in that respect. We do as of this moment, Mr. President and Your Honours, we do not have any witnesses available for next week. With respect to the information concerning the intercepts, we will be making that information available, I anticipate, on Monday or Tuesday of next week. Ms. Karper, our former case manager, is working on the missing documents, and my understanding is that she will be providing some of that material to the legal officer later today. Among the documents which are not yet available, of course, are those for which we are awaiting translation, but my understanding is those documents should be available one week from today. The final issue I need to bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber and the Defence concerns the order that we designate or determine who would be the appropriate witnesses to authenticate the documents. Late yesterday afternoon I received a spreadsheet based on the contested exhibit spreadsheet that was previously provided on the 8th -- on the 19th of April. Two analysts from our team have identified the likely Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authenticating witnesses for about 600 of the 660 contested documents. A number of those documents have been withdrawn, so the number is slightly less than 660. There are a few documents that we are still unable to identify an authenticating witness for. I regret to inform the Trial Chamber, however, that having analysed the names of the individuals who are listed as authenticating witnesses, the total number is 163 witnesses, which clearly is not possible or reasonable for us to bring before this Trial Chamber. I will also add, Mr. President, that 105 of those witnesses would be able to authenticate only one document. What we are attempting to do is formulate some ideas as to perhaps other means to solve this problem, whether it's calling an analyst or analysts from within the Office of the Prosecutor who could provide a document type of analysis, in terms of the context of the documents, and someone who has familiarity with the large number of documents in order to determine whether or not they are authentic. Another option, of course, would be to call a number of witnesses who could authenticate large numbers of the documents, such as, for example, one of the witnesses that was identified, we believe, could authenticate approximately 130 of the documents. But I also should bring to the attention of the Trial Chamber and the Defence that it appears to us that a significant number of the witnesses that might be necessary for authentication purposes could be Defence witnesses in this case, which might raise other issues pertaining to bringing them here for the limited purpose of authenticating documents. Again, we are in the process of formulating some proposed suggestions on how to deal with this problem, particularly in light of the fact that as Your Honours are aware, the Prosecution was not clearly put on notice that authenticity would be an issue until relatively late in these proceedings and certainly not at the pre-trial stage of this case. I anticipate that we will file the spreadsheet containing the lists, again, either Monday or Tuesday, and I anticipate appending to that some proposed suggestions or ideas as to how to solve this problem, which the Prosecution clearly recognises is one that is a very difficult situation for the Trial Chamber and the parties. That summarises the position with respect to the ongoing projects pertaining to the oral order. I should also mention one final thing: Your Honours had asked us to, in effect, sequence the documents to determine whether it's possible to determine if documents were sent or received based on the chain of the documents. That project is ongoing, and I will brief you as to when that information will be available and in what format it will be available as soon as I have a better idea as to when that information will be available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. I'm now going to give the floor to the Defence. There were a number of points that you raised and addressed. First of all, the question -- we've dealt with the question of signatures. Now, what remains are the hearings for June. You said that there was a week, from the 21st of June is what I heard, so I assume that's from the 21st to the 28th, that week, that's what you mean, that we have envisaged Judge Adamovic, plus an archivist and other witnesses. You told us that for the following week there is nothing that has been envisaged, so between the 14th and the 21st of June, what's happening during that week? That's what I'm wondering. Now, as to the following week, to next week, if we don't manage to complete the videotapes by the end of the day today, of course we shall continue on Monday, during our Monday hearing. Now, if we do get through all the videotapes today, then we won't be sitting from Monday to Friday, if you say there are no witnesses. But what happens with the week after? You didn't indicate anything. Theoretically speaking, it should have been the witnesses we mentioned yesterday, and I don't want to say anything about that in open session. So I'm going to give you the floor again with respect to planning and scheduling, in view of the fact that we have no hearings next week because there are no witnesses, unless we continue with our business on Monday, not having finished today. Now, the Court witnesses come the following week, and afterwards the archivist and Mr. Adamovic and perhaps some other witnesses too. Is that what we can expect and understand? And in the list you have not included your -- Mr. Tauru for the famous sketches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, by our estimate, we have remaining between 8 and 12 witnesses to testify in total. That includes the Court witness, two to three archivists, Judge Adamovic, Mika Tauru, the two witnesses who were the subject of the videolink decision, one or perhaps two witnesses yet to be determined who will address the issue of orders, transmission of orders, delegation of authority, et cetera, which the Chamber has ordered us to produce. I failed to mention that we have requested the Bosnian government to assist us in that endeavour, and we have yet to receive a response from them. As Your Honour knows, we have also previously indicated that we will be making an application to add one witness in the form of the investigative team leader, who will testify about efforts undertaken to obtain certain records that would be of assistance or could be relevant to these proceedings. That witness has yet to finalise his statement primarily because he is currently in Bosnia undertaking efforts that will be the subject of his proposed testimony. So what we would propose, Mr. President, is that in the week following the Court witness, that is, the week of the 21st, we will have the two to three archivists, Judge Adamovic, and perhaps, if time permits, because he normally is here in the building, our investigative team leader, who of course can be called on short notice because he works here in the building. Then the following week, being the week of the 28th, we hopefully will be in a position to call Mr. Tauru, and hopefully by that point in time the issue concerning one of the videolink witnesses might be resolved. We will, of course, endeavour to bring those witnesses here, if their medical conditions permit, by the end of this month; if not, we will have to revisit the issue of the videolinks, and then of course the one or two witnesses pursuant to the Trial Chamber's order concerning the issuing of orders within the ABiH. So it is possible that with a bit of good luck, in terms of witness availability, and moving as expeditiously as possible, that we may be in a position whereby the week of the 28th of June would be the final witnesses for the Prosecution. As Your Honours are well aware, the Prosecution position is that we are not in a position to close our case until the issue of the contested documents has been resolved. I don't anticipate there being any change in that position. So that if we finish with witnesses by, say, the 2nd of July, we would then be waiting a Trial Chamber decision on the admissibility of the contested documents, and that would be the only thing that would be hindering us from closing our case at that -- at that point. That's about as much information as I'm able to provide, Your Honours, at this point in time, but we are hopeful that we will be able to complete the oral testimony of the witnesses by the week of the 28th of June or perhaps into the -- the first few days of the following week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you for those explanations. You also said, as far as the telephone intercepts were concerned, that you would disclose the missing documents next week; that is to say, the missing transcripts in both languages. With regard to the documents, you said that you are establishing a spreadsheet, that you are drawing up a spreadsheet and you would provide us with it in the near future. As far as the orders are concerned, you said that you had contacted the BH government in order to obtain information about how within the BH army orders might be transmitted. To this effect, you said Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that the Trial Chamber had requested that a witness be called who could inform the Chamber about how orders were transmitted in the field and so that he could inform the Chamber of all technical issues. You said that you have examined this question. According to your calculations, with regard to the 600 documents -- there are about 600 documents that could be dealt with through this witness, if you find this witness. You said that there are about 163 documents too, but only certain witnesses could testify with regard to one document. You have, on the other hand, one witness who could authenticate 130 documents. That's what you said. But you also raised another issue, and you said that this member of the military, who would come to testify here, could be considered as a Defence witness, in your opinion. As a result, you have proposed two solutions: Either we should hear an analyst from the OTP, or we should call this witness after all. I'd like to point out that when a witness makes the solemn declaration, he becomes a witness for the Court and that changes many things. The witness we are requesting is one we would like not to ask him questions -- one we would like to have not to ask him questions about the substance but about orders. We would like to know how orders are made, how they are sent; we would like to know who received the orders; we'd like to know whether there were faxes, whether couriers were used to transmit orders or electronic means. There's an entire series of purely technical questions, and this would not make it necessary for the witness to side with the Defence or the Prosecution, because this witness would only be answering questions of a technical nature, and this is why the question as to whether the witness might be one for the Defence, in my opinion, is not a question that should prevent us from calling a member of the military to testify about the procedure followed. Naturally, you will continue to work on this matter. We, the Judges, will discuss it and bear in mind the fact that you have suggested that an analyst be called rather than a witness; although in its oral decision the Trial Chamber wanted a member of the military to testify. We'll bear in mind what you have said, and the Judges will discuss the matter. Naturally, within the framework of the adversarial proceedings, the Trial Chamber would also like to hear what the Defence's position is. I will let the Defence take the floor, unless there is something that Mr. Mundis would like to add. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let me just attempt to clarify one point where perhaps earlier I may have misspoken or may not have made myself clear. There are two distinct issues that are involved with respect to the authentication of the documents: The first one is the ABiH commander or senior military officer who could testify about the orders, how they were transmitted, and those type of technical issues. That's who the Prosecution has sought the assistance of the Bosnian government, simply based on the outstanding protocols whereby any currently serving member of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or any government official, we must go through the Bosnian government prior to directly contacting such individuals. That issue is, the Prosecution would submit, a separate issue from the witnesses who could authenticate all of the documents, and it's with respect to the authenticating witnesses that we have identified 163 people, which is clearly an excessive number, and it was with respect to that portion that one of our proposals that we will submit next week might be for an analyst within the Office of the Prosecutor to discuss. We're not varying or seeking variation of your order that we call in addition to that a senior member of the ABiH to explain technical issues concerning orders. We clearly make a distinction between those two things. It's with respect to solving the problem of avoiding 163 witnesses having to come in, of whom 105 would only be able to authenticate one document. That's what we clearly are not going to be able to do. And it's with respect to that that we will be making some proposals next week that will include having an analyst or analysts testify in court about the conclusions that they have reached based on their professional training as analysts in evaluating the contested documents and putting those documents into the context of other events that have happened and the evidence that's currently before Your Honours. So if I wasn't clear before, Mr. President, we are clearly making a distinction between those two different, very different types of evidence, one concerning authentication and one concerning the technical issues of how orders were transmitted, delegation authorities, et cetera, that was clearly set forth in the Chamber's oral order of 17 May. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis, for these explanations. I'll now turn to the Defence to hear what their position is with regard to all the issues that Mr. Mundis has discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Good day, Madam Judge. Good day, Your Honour. The Defence's comments will be quite brief. First of all, I'd like to thank my colleague from the Prosecution for all the information that he has just provided us with, with all the information about what the Trial Chamber requested that he do with regard to the admissibility of documents. The only issue I'd like to raise concerns the authentication of documents and the number of witnesses that the Prosecution said should be called to authenticate documents. The Defence doesn't want to cause any difficulties. We would like to facilitate the Prosecution's work. We suggest that we meet members of the Prosecution as soon as possible in order to try and find a solution so that we can facilitate the proceedings, and naturally in doing so we will try to defend the accused's rights. So we suggest that we do this as soon as possible. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. And the other Defence team, Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, on the point of the documents that were submitted with the accused's signatures on, I did want to indicate for the record that there's no objection to those documents being formally tendered. And indeed, Your Honours will know when we were discussing the documents, we did indicate on behalf of Mr. Kubura what his signature was on one of the documents, so there's no dispute about this matter. Then the other matter, Your Honours, is just with regard to the -- the scheduling. If there are no witnesses available for next week, we would request that the Prosecution seek as soon as possible - and I know, of course, they will do this - to provide statements for the witnesses who are to come the week thereafter and after that, so that the time can be used, especially if the documents need to be translated, to prepare for -- for those witnesses, because these would all be new statements that we will be getting from the Prosecution. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Mundis [sic]. With regard to all the issues raised by the Prosecution, the Defence said that on the whole they were glad to receive the information provided by the Prosecution. Mr. Bourgon said that as far as the authenticity of documents are concerned - and naturally, he said he didn't want to obstruct the proceedings but would nevertheless like to defend the accused's rights - Mr. Bourgon said he would like to meet with the Prosecution in order to find a solution to the question of authenticity and the question of a witness who might be able to come to authenticate the documents. Naturally, the Trial Chamber supports this suggestion if a consensus can be reached by the parties. In addition, the Defence said that they would like to have by the 21st of June the written statements in order to be able to prepare for the testimony of these witnesses. We have more or less dealt with all these issues. Mr. Mundis, would you like to take the floor again? But I should point out that after the break, we will render our decision on the question of the admissibility of the two files that relate to the signatures of the accused. Mr. Mundis, is there anything you would like to say in response to what Defence counsel has just said?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to witness statements, we of course will make those available as soon as we have them. The current plan is for Ms. Benjamin to return to The Hague this weekend. I would expect, therefore, certainly some witness statements, additional witness statements, will be available perhaps as early as late Monday. We, of course, have to enter them into our evidence system before they can be disclosed, but we can certainly expedite that process, and I would anticipate that by Tuesday of next week at the latest there should be some statements available pertaining to the witnesses that would be coming the week of the 21st.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Just -- there's just something else I would like to add. I forgot to mention something. This is something that the Defence missed. You suggested to have a chief of investigations come to testify. This witness would testify about investigations independently of Mr. Tauru. Naturally, this seems very suitable for the Chamber, if an investigator comes to say how he worked, if he says what the mission he had was, if he told us how the statements were taken, and if we can be told why the documents weren't tendered with the written statements, given that they were original documents. There is an entire series of questions that could be raised in the course of such testimony. As far as calling a chief of investigations is concerned, what is the Defence's position, who will naturally be able to cross-examine this witness? Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. This naturally depends on the contents of the investigator's statement. If we had his statement, we would know the points -- the issues about which he would like to testify. But there's the question of documents. My colleague mentioned that the chief of investigations was in Bosnia in order to prepare testimony. I don't know whether the chief of investigations is searching for new documents or not, but if there are new documents that might be produced by this witness, we would like to be informed about this as soon as possible. Perhaps I have misunderstood this, but the fact that he is in Bosnia to prepare his testimony might mean that he is searching for new documents. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, as far as the chief of investigations is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may assist in clarifying the origin of many of these documents. But as Mr. Bourgon said, it depends entirely on what the investigator does know and what he's able to put in a statement. If such a statement is being prepared - and I understand it is along similar lines - it's then a matter that the Defence can review. But our position would remain that with regard to the documents themselves, especially the internal military documents, that we do need witnesses who can authenticate the origin of those documents, as Your Honours have ordered. A investigator statement might go some way to addressing that matter. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As far as this issue is concerned, the Defence has mentioned two problems, which are important ones. First of all, would this investigator testify within the framework of a previous statement that he would have made? And naturally, such statement should be provided to the Defence so that they can examine it. But the second problem, which is also important, is would this investigator be used by the Prosecution to tender new documents? The Trial Chamber would like more information with regard to all these problems. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the investigation team leader is currently in Bosnia with an investigative team, again going through court records and district military prosecutor's records in order to hopefully satisfy the Chamber that steps were not taken by units of the 3rd Corps to punish the perpetrators of the crimes that are set forth in the indictment. So the point is not for the investigator to return with a large number of documents but precisely the opposite. The team that is currently searching through, again, the court archives is attempting to demonstrate that there are no such records pertaining to the crimes that are set forth in the Third Amended Indictment. The subject matter of that proposed testimony would be to the effect that teams of investigators have again gone through the court records, and there are no records indicating that the crimes in the Third Amended Indictment were the subject of referrals by the 3rd Corps or its subordinate units. So it's not a question of coming back with additional documents; it's a question of testifying as to the lack thereof. Once that mission is complete, the investigative team leader will compile or finalise a statement that will set forth for Your Honours all the efforts made by the Office of the Prosecutor with respect to that issue, and he will then be made available to testify and answer questions of the Defence and the Trial Chamber with respect to those efforts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Trial Chamber has understood this correctly, the investigation team leader is now in Bosnia and Herzegovina with his team, and he's in contact with various courts, military or civilian courts, from the time in order -- he's consulting archives in order to verify whether any procedures were followed that might support what is stated in the amended indictment. And having completed his work, the investigator would be called, and in the course of an examination-in-chief you'd question the witness about his work and the conclusions he reached. This is what you have told us. Having heard those explanations, I will give the floor to the Defence again.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Naturally, the Defence isn't surprised to hear that the Prosecution is following this method, because not long ago they admitted all the measures that were taken in the 3rd Corps with regard to a multitude of events in 1993. So now we're looking for exceptions rather than the rule. So we can understand the position of the OTP. Nevertheless, we would like to underline the fact that by carrying out such searches, any documents of an exculpatory nature for the accused or any documents that might diminish evidence of the Prosecution should be provided to us in accordance with the Rule, and according to what the Prosecution has said, it is our understanding that a number of documents could be provided to us on the basis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I think there are two separate matters here, Your Honour. The one is the investigator looking at measures. And I understand there will be a statement produced along those lines and an application to add that witness to the witness list. And once that happens, then the Defence can respond to that new statement, and as Your Honours say, if the witness is to be called, cross-examine the witness on that point. The other matter is whether an investigator or analyst would be called to assist in the authentication of the documents, and on that point my submission earlier was that our position remains that the witnesses who were actually involved in the production and distribution of those documents should be called as the best evidence available. But an investigator or analyst may be able to assist, depending on what's in his statement with the authentication process, and we have to wait to see what the Prosecution proposal is before we respond to that. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In the light of what the Defence has just said, there is one issue that stands out; it was mentioned by Mr. Bourgon. If this investigator came across documents of an exculpatory nature for the accused, in such a case the Prosecution should disclose these documents to the Defence, pursuant to Rule 68. That's what was said. Mr. Mundis, what could you tell the Defence about this matter? What could you tell them about what would happen if the investigator discovered material of an exculpatory nature?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is -- there is no doubt such material would in fact be disclosed to the Defence. And I neglected to mention that earlier. Let me also say in this respect that later this morning the Prosecution will be seeking specific information from the Defence with respect to potential Rule 68 material. And I have a letter that I will be handing to both Defence counsel later this morning, perhaps during the first break, that specifically addresses this issue, which is not one that was unanticipated or certainly is one that we anticipated in this context. And so we are actually seeking some assistance from the Defence in order to actively search for material that might fall within Rule 68. But certainly anything that comes within our possession will be disclosed to the Defence as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for these submissions. The Defence will consult with the Prosecution about the matter. We've spent almost an hour on dealing with these problems. We could perhaps continue with the viewing of the videotapes. I'll give the floor to the Prosecution now. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. With your leave, Mr. Ruxton will now depart the courtroom, and I will once again turn over the presentation of the videos to my colleague, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Neuner, you may take the floor. The Trial Chamber greets you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Defence counsel and everybody in and around the courtroom. I want to start by distributing the -- a list containing the order of sequences which will be displayed. If I may ask the usher. We have also, I hope, enough copies for the translators. What Your Honours can see from this order list is the following: That we are continuing with showing a video which we couldn't see yesterday afternoon, and I want your -- I want to point your attention to point 5 here on the list. This is a video about which we talked with the Defence this morning again. This is the video with the ERN number V0003971. It is a video which is about detention facilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina allegedly held by -- or allegedly run by the ABiH or associate forces. Basically it's a compilation of footage taken on the -- in April 2002 by Marinus Dorrestijn, who helped the Office of the Prosecutor in shooting footage about all of the detention facilities listed in the indictment; namely, relating to paragraph 28, paragraph 41 till 43 of the indictment. This videotape, which would have 97 minutes of footage about the detention facility, we agreed with the Defence that the audio of this tape would be removed, and therefore under the condition that we say it was taken in April 2002, we agreed that it is not necessary to show this video in its entirety in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I can also inform Your Honours that the stills which were shown to numerous witnesses by the Prosecution in the course of these proceedings were always taken from this video. On the video itself, when the individual detention facilities are shown, there is also a kind of display, a kind of name what detention facility it relates to, so that the Defence pointed that out, it is not necessary to have the audio, which would also explain what detention facility it is, and we agreed to remove the audio in order to tender it this way so that we don't have to screen it this morning. If I may move on. Under point 5.1, on the bottom of the page which was just distributed, this is another video which comes from the reserve list, and for the time being it is still on the reserve list. This is the video with the ERN number V0004306. This video carries also the PT number 1138, or the P number 63. This is a video shown to Nenad Bogeljic, the witness Nenad Bogeljic, on the 28th of January of this year, transcript pages 2.123 for following. I checked the transcript yesterday, and Mr. Bogeljic had identified four persons who received beatings in Motel Sretno prior to 20th of May, 1993, so four of the numerous persons or victims shown on this tape have been identified already as having been in the Motel Sretno, and I -- or the Prosecution wishes to leave it to Your Honours whether you wish to see this video in its entirety, which is 62 minutes in its duration, or the relevant excerpt would be 62 minutes in its duration; the whole video would be two hours, nine minutes, but the selected relevant portion would be 62 minutes. However, the Prosecution wishes to state that the victims are also interviewed on this tape, and for this reason we have for the time being left it on the reserve list, because there would be no possibility for the Defence to cross-examine the other victims shown on this tape. If I can seek guidance from Your Honour in relation to this tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will tell you after the break what our decision will be. Now, with respect to the reserve video lasting 62 minutes, you say, what is the position of the Defence on that particular videotape?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. With respect to your first question, I would rather cede the floor to my colleague representing Mr. Kubura. But I would like to make certain comments with respect to the number 5 exhibit which was mentioned, and we wanted to know whether that will -- exhibit will be tendered, the videotape concerning the places and different places in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But we should also like to mention that it is a videotape which was taped in the year 2001 and that that particular videotape has nothing to do with the situation and state of affairs which existed in those facilities in 1993. The facilities were clearly identified on that videotape, and the Trial Chamber will be able to see, for example, that if a videotape is mentioned, if it was taken, that then the videotape shows the name of the facility as well. And my learned colleague mentioned the detention facilities. But we would like to speak about the other facilities that the witnesses mentioned during their testimony here possibly, and it is up to the Trial Chamber to decide how they're going to characterise those locations and facilities that we can see on the footage. But the essential point, Your Honours, is that the agreement reached between the Defence and Prosecution has to do to the audiotapes -- or rather, the soundtrack, the comments accompanying the videotape. And we have proceeded in a similar fashion before when we had videotapes on which we were able to see the consequences of the abduction of Mr. Totic, and the Prosecution accepted that the soundtrack be removed. So we had nothing against having the images exhibited, and we did so in a similar case. So there have been cases of this kind when we object to the acceptability of certain videotapes, apart from the fact that the witness was already before the Trial Chamber. We were not able to cross-examine him about his conception of the videotapes. Then the comment that was heard in our opinion is usually the main obstacle to having the tape exhibited, tendered and accepted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, thank you. Let's hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. With respect to videotape number 5, Your Honours, the problem with the audio was that there was a lot of commentary and interpretation of events, and that, as Your Honour knows, is a matter that we have objected to, and the Prosecution have agreed to remove those -- those comments, and it's for that reason that there's no objection to the video therefore being tendered with only the images, as Mr. Bourgon has said. It's a matter for Your Honours whether it's necessary, therefore, to view it all in public or whether that could be viewed out of court, if it is then tendered into -- to evidence. Your Honours, in respect of the final video, 5.1, I understand that this is the entire video of which certain excerpts have already been admitted into evidence, without any sound, and that was done in order, once again, to avoid the commentary being made. Our position would be that the Defence had the opportunity then -- sorry, the Prosecution had the opportunity then, if they wanted to introduce any further portions of the video, to do that through that witness or other witnesses, and that the balance of the video should not, therefore, now be admitted, certainly if it contains scenes of interviews with witnesses where we are not going to have an opportunity to -- to cross-examine those witnesses. So in our submission, the relevant portions, according to the Prosecution, have been admitted already through a witness, and the rest of the video should -- should not be admitted, and there's no need therefore to show it if it contains scenes with commentary and interviews that it's going to be impossible for the Defence to test at this stage. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As concerns the reserve video, was this video on the list of exhibits, contested exhibits, or is it a video -- an additional video that was not on the original list that was contested? I'd like to hear your positions on that point. And if it was on the list, what was its number?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, like all the videos, also this video has been contested, and it has the contested number 407. The pre-trial number is 1138.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I did check that out just now, and the number is 407. That's quite right. It was PTW 1113. But anyway, thank you for clearing that point up. We still have 20 minutes left. Can we go ahead with the short excerpts?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next tape -- or an excerpt from the next tape has been shown yesterday already, so I will reduce the background information on this videotape because it has been given already yesterday. The ERN number of the tape is V0002401. For the translators, a summary translation is contained in tab number 19 of the binder. 15 minutes -- we should be able to see the 15 minutes of the second excerpt, running from 26 minutes up to 41 minutes 20 of this tape. It shows the exchange of Mr. Totic, on the one hand side, and of the Mujahedin, on the other hand side, in Zenica, and at the beginning also some footage of the Mujahedin which are being brought to the exchange is being shown. The tape will be played now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. We have 15 minutes, so that makes everything fine.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] What are you going to say when you come to Zenica about the behaviour of these -- Blazo, bring it over here. Are they going to come here again? You wait. Wait for a while. Don't go yet. Wait. Close the door. Did they admit -- What? Did they admit they were guilty? Stay away from the window so that they cannot see us. Keep quiet. It's not on now. Listen, bring me a battery. Only, take it easy so they do not see what you're carrying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The videotape -- the impression we gain from viewing the videotape is the following: It would appear that we have a juxtaposition of sequences coming from different sources, a compilation. The first source -- in the first sequence, we see the Mujahedin being detained in a place with agents -- with guards present. It says, "HVO Dom." We see that. And we see the individuals wearing white jogging attire coming out of their cells, so they are being held in a facility with cells, in a building with cells. And we see that they are speaking amongst themselves. They don't seem to be particularly anxious. And then we see the arrival of a white truck or vehicle. Then we see a sequence where they are arriving at some other location, and there is some Red Cross vehicles there as well as some blue helmets. After that, we see another sequence, another passage, which shows that it is a compilation, a collage. We see Commander Totic, embracing certain individuals, probably family members, and he is getting into a Red Cross vehicle. And then the third excerpt has a commentary in Arabic. And although we do not understand Arabic, I was able to distinguish very precisely the following words: "Croatia, Zenica, commander," et cetera, in Arabic. And we see on the sequence a logo; it says, "QP." It is the logo on the left, so it's probably the channel broadcasting this excerpt or the producer. We see a number of events taking place before our eyes. First of all, we see Commander Totic with some soldiers around him. Then there is a sequence where we see some Mujahedin -- hostages with the Mujahedin surrounded and they're entering a building -- or rather, the hotel building, and we see the hostages getting into the vehicle with Totic and being taken off somewhere where they'll be freed. Then we have another sequence, where we see the soldiers dressed in battle dress, and we see very distinctly a lance rocket insignia [as interpreted]. This is visible. And we also see UN vehicles which took part in the exchange. They took part in an active fashion. And we see the alleged freeing of the Mujahedin, and they're all displaying their happiness, and it is part of the sequence we saw yesterday. So that in the roughest of terms is what we were able to see viewing the videotape, and it incorporated a number of elements. Would the Defence like to say anything for a few minutes before the break, or would you prefer to do it after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps five minutes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll do that after the break, as it is now time for our break. We'll have our break, and we'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll now resume. But before we start viewing the videos, the Trial Chamber will render a number of decisions that regard various issues. First of all, with regard to the videotape 5.1, the so-called reserve tape, the Trial Chamber believes that it is not necessary to show this tape. The decision concerning the viewing of this videotape will be taken at a later date, but we for the moment are not authorising the broadcasting of this tape. As far as tape 5 is concerned, which relates to the detention facilities, this was a tape made in 2001, the Trial Chamber -- in 2002. The Trial Chamber notes that there was an agreement reached between the Prosecution and the Defence, and they agreed that the tape should be withdrawn. In order to save time, the Trial Chamber believes that it would be best not to show this 97-minute tape. The Trial Chamber will view it themselves. So tape number 5 will not be shown today. In addition, questions about the transcripts of the Dusina and Vares tapes were not dealt with yesterday. These are tapes that were produced in other cases, and their transcripts form part of the record of other cases. At this point in time, the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that the Defence should have these transcripts in their possession, and it is for the Prosecution to provide the Defence with these transcripts. Once the Defence has these transcripts in its possession, they will inform the Trial Chamber of all the questions that arise as a result of an examination of these transcripts, and they will inform the Trial Chamber of the useful questions that they would have put to the witness had the witness been present. Once the Trial Chamber has heard the Defence's point of view and the point of view of the Prosecution in the light of the Defence's comments, the Trial Chamber will then deliberate. The Trial Chamber will then render a ruling. And the last issue I'd like to address: As far as next week is concerned, as we have said, no witnesses have been scheduled for next week, so there won't be any hearings. But given that a number of questions -- a number of issues have to be raised with the Trial Chamber, and in particular the question of the archivists and other problems, the Trial Chamber believes that on Wednesday at 9.00 we should have a hearing. So we will only have a hearing on Wednesday. During this hearing, we'll take stock of the situation and deal with all the issues that have not yet been solved. And finally, the last question that has to be dealt with - and the Trial Chamber has just deliberated about the matter - concerns the signatures. The Trial Chamber has decided to admit into evidence the two files compiled by the Prosecution, who have one file, number 1, which contains documents bearing the original signatures of the accused General Hadzihasanovic. I will now ask the registrar to give us an exhibit number for this document. And the second file contains documents bearing the original signatures of Mr. Kubura. So I will also ask the registrar to provide me with an exhibit number for the second file. I'm going to provide these files to the registrar now, and you will give me exhibit numbers for these files.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These documents will be given a P number, and in addition they will be under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the first file that relates to Mr. Hadzihasanovic will be number P113, under seal; and file number 2, which relates to the accused Kubura, the number will be P114, under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are then the decisions that the Trial Chamber has rendered. We will now continue with the viewing of the videotapes that remain to be seen and which are referred to in the spreadsheet provided a while ago. Before we do so, the Defence should inform us of their position with regard to the video that we saw before the break. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The comments concerning the last tape that we viewed -- first of all, my comment concerns an observation of the Trial Chamber about what was seen in the tape. The Trial Chamber noted that we saw Mujahedin in a building which seems to be a place where there were cells. I think it's important to point out, Mr. President, that we don't know whether the people we saw in the video were in fact Mujahedin. We have certain information and evidence concerning these persons, naturally if the individuals we saw are the individuals mentioned by the witnesses in the course of these proceedings. Those would be my preliminary remarks. Mr. President, although we see in the first sequence the inside of a building and then we see the outside and a white van people are entering, although we see this, we don't know where the site is nor do we know who the people are who appear at that site. Similarly, we don't know, as the Trial Chamber has pointed out -- we can't see the guards in charge of these people, if there were any such guards; and also, the question is if there were any guards, the video must have been made with their agreement. So there's a number of questions that haven't been answered, and we only have a minimum of information in relation to the first sequence. As far as the second sequence is concerned, Mr. President, we can see a Red Cross vehicle in the sequence. Naturally, we don't know whether the Red Cross was actually present. We can see some blue helmets, but we do not know where this site is. All we can do is imagine that perhaps this is the site referred to as the site which was one of the meeting places, but we have no information about this. As far as the third site is concerned, naturally the Trial Chamber concluded that we were able to recognise a site in front of a hotel in Zenica. We have already had the opportunity of seeing this site in the past when evidence was presented. But the people we see in the video, yet again there is only one person among them whom we can recognise, and this person is Mr. Totic. Naturally, we can see two individuals dressed in white, which might lead us to believe that these individuals are EU Monitoring Mission representatives, but we do not know their identity. There is perhaps another person that we might think we know; it's the first person who seems to be getting out of a UN vehicle, and this seems to be a person who appears in a photograph that was tendered into evidence through the last witness. Namely -- this would be a Mujahedin. We might think that this person is a Mujahedin. These comments on the third sites in these -- on the three sites in these three sequences show that we don't have enough information to use this video in any way as evidence in these proceedings. Naturally, the question of the source is still one that we have to ask ourselves about. We don't know what the source is; we don't know when it was made; we don't know when the sequences were filmed; we don't know when the video was compiled; and we do not have any witnesses who would be able to come to authenticate this material or to describe at least the scenes depicted in the video. Even the witness Totic, who has testified before this Chamber, was not able to describe anything other than the site where apparently he met people whom he recognised, and he wasn't able to say anything, apart from the time when he was in Zenica. He wasn't able to say anything about people leaving a building to enter a vehicle. As far as the English text is concerned, which we were provided with under tab 19, when comments come from people who are actors in the tape, naturally the Defence can listen to what these people say and they can bear this in mind, but any other comments that appear in the transcript - and for example, in line 37.56 we have a description according to which an EU monitor supervises the transfer of Totic from a Mujahedin vehicle to a UN vehicle - this commentary, Mr. President, is a commentary made by someone whose identity is unknown. Was it by someone from the Prosecution? We do not know how this commentary was added to the line 37.56. And, Mr. President, another comment was added to the tape. It's not even a part of the tape. It seems that they say that there was a Mr. Mahmuljin and Alagic who assisted, who were present at a gathering of Mujahedin, and there were words spoken in Arabic. This part is not part of the video; it's a different sequence. And we don't know why at 48.17, this line, this comment appears. We do not know the source of this comment. And for these reasons, Mr. President, we believe that this is evidence that is being suggested but it does not have sufficient reliability to allow the Judges to draw any conclusions, and it cannot assist the Judges in determining matters that are in dispute in these proceedings. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. The other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Apart from the comments set forth by Mr. Bourgon, there is nothing we would like to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. I will give the floor to the Prosecution again, if the Prosecution would like to respond to what the Defence has just stated. The Defence has pointed out that in their opinion nothing in the cassette, nothing in the tape allows one to say that the people we see coming out of this facility, in which there are cells, and the people who are liberated are Mujahedin. That is the Defence's interpretation. Nothing allows us to claim that these individuals are Mujahedin. Would the Prosecution like to respond, or shall we start viewing the next video?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I could make a brief comment. First of all, the Prosecution has never alleged that we would know the source, or we have made it quite clear from the beginning that this -- these excerpts just being shown, that we don't know the originator. Since these Mujahedin in the detention facility before the HVO Dom sign is being shown have full beards, it is practically impossible to make a comparison between the stills drawn from the faces when they are in the detention facility and later on at the exchange. With regard to the scene shown from Mr. Totic, the witness Totic has stated that this was at the prisoner exchange or at the way [sic] in the vehicle to the prisoner exchange, which took place in Zenica on the 17th of May, 1993. However, during the proofing and before we realised that since he was just part on one side of the exchange, he certainly was not in a position to testify about the other side of the prisoner exchange, meaning the Mujahedin. He even, while the exchange was taking place, was not meeting this group at all. For this reason, we made, while the witness Totic was here in front of Your Honours, we made the decision not to show the full sequence. Finally, I want to say we fully agree with the summary made by Your Honours immediately after the tape has been shown, and we would now proceed with the next video screening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have taken note of what you have just said. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very briefly. I would just like to point out that as far as the individuals are concerned in the video, if these are people who appear in a photograph, the only witness who was heard before this Chamber was the last witness, who said that these were members of the mission; they weren't Mujahedin, he said. We can say that they appear to be foreigners in Bosnia, but the witness said that they were involved in a mission. He said they weren't Mujahedin. There's a distinction to be made. Mr. President, when Mr. Totic testified, as far as I can remember, he did not mention that before he was liberated he met people close to him, which is in the manner depicted in the cassette. We don't know whether this is the same event or another event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for all these explanations provided by both sides, by both parties. We should now continue with the viewing of the videos. I'll give the floor to the Prosecution, who will inform us about the video that we are now going to view.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The next sequence is taken from the same tape, so I will not give additional information on the author, the source or submitter of the tape, and the manner in which it was received, because this was done earlier. The sequence is undated, and it is short, about three minutes. The first 30 seconds relate to another excerpt, and basically in the copying process the first 30 seconds were just copied with this as a kind of security matter to -- in order to -- we always start to show a few seconds -- a few seconds before the actual sequence. The video as such is of bad quality. What can be seen on the upper left-hand side is a "QP," a symbol "QP," which is basically the same -- or points to a kind of TV station from the same -- which is -- this excerpt is taken from the same excerpt like the previous one. And the Prosecution believes this is the video footage about the Battalion Jihad. There are some flags or a kind of poster shown on which the Arabic word and below in the letters "Battalion Jihad" are written. The sequence will be played now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We'll discuss it later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This tape, which lasts for several minutes, is the continuation of the video that we saw a while ago, since the logo is the same. There is a commentary in Arabic. It's a pity that we didn't have the English translation of this commentary in the Arabic language. We can see some soldiers who apparently don't have any insignia on them. And in one of the first sequences we can see three lines and there are eight men in each line, so there's a minimum of 24 individuals. I counted the number of lines. I heard the word "Mujahedin" in the Arabic language. I would like to draw this to the attention -- I would like to draw your attention to this. If you desire, if the Defence desires that we review the cassette, we can do so. The commentator said the word "Mujahedin." There are a number of benches and tables in the video. This is certainly a place where the people ate. They are lined up in three lines. In each line, there are eight individuals. There are apparently some officers who are observing the -- or other people who are observing them. Then there is a march that is not very organised. The soldiers are marching in all directions and they cry out, et cetera. We can see a sort of a large or long flag with inscriptions which we could not see or read. And we can also see in the background a wood -- a wooden house. That's what we could say about the video we have just seen. Is there anything the Defence would like to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The first remark is this: We do not know who the people are whom we see on the videotape. We do not know what the location is. We don't know whether we're in Bosnia or in another country, not even that. And there is a sequence where it seems that there are some superior officers sitting down on a bench looking at something. We can see quite clearly that it is a collage. Now, whether they were facing the three columns or whether they were somewhere else, we can't tell. The word "Mujahedin" was heard in the commentary in Arabic. Now, the word "Mujahedin" is applied almost everywhere in the world and there are Mujahedins everywhere, so where this was, we still don't know. It was no indication. Then there was the flag. We saw something that looked like "Jihad." Of course, Jihads are waged all over the world, so that doesn't point to the exact location either. And in the absence of a witness to explain to us what this is all about, the Defence really doesn't see how this video can be useful to the Chamber at all, to help you decide and reach your decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. What about the other Defence lawyers. Mr. Ibrisimovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Mr. President, we have no further comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would the Prosecution like to respond to the remarks made by the Defence, with respect to the fact that there's no date, there's no location cited, and all the other incertitudes that were quoted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution could proceed as such that we view the next and even the following sequence, which are more or less drawn from the same event. The next sequence is a little bit longer. This sequence was just two minutes, and the next is about five minutes. It's of worse condition. However, it shows, again, the flag. And the third sequence is also drawn from the same event. We could also make a comment now, but we could reserve it for later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if you group your comments in a general manner, we can hear them after the sequences.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So we are continuing. The next videotape is V0001737. As I said, it's the longest sequence, running from one hour 30 minutes till one hour 35 minutes, about five minutes from a tape which has a duration of two hours and 43 minutes. I also said it had a bad or worse image, a bad image. At the beginning, we have, again, the previous -- previous footage about other events. We see, again, these soldiers, eight soldiers standing next to each other, but the relevant sequence is the event, where again the flag is being shown. The submitter of -- okay, the author of this tape is also unknown. It was submitted to us by Bozo Pavlovic. And we will show the video now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] The future is uncertain. People from the whole world have united. We are extreme. We are extremists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This part of the tape follows on from the videotape that we saw a moment ago, with the same people present. We can see a banner where it says "Brigada Jihad," that is legible, "Brigada Jihad" on the banner. And then there is a speech being delivered by someone. We don't know who that someone is, of course. Is it a religious leader? Is it a military leader or somebody else? We cannot know that. Facing the soldiers who could be new recruits or young recruits there are other people sitting down, some of them in military uniform, and everybody is listening to a speech being delivered. As to the location, we can see that behind the location there is a hill and there are trees on the hill. It is not winter; that is obvious. Maybe it is spring and maybe it is summer, but certainly not winter and certainly not autumn. So those are basically the observations that one can make having viewed that excerpt. Mr. Bourgon, would you like to make your observations at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just very rapidly. What we can see having seen the videotape: It is a collage, once again, a compilation of different scenes, a juxtaposition. So that conclusion is drawn on the fact that there are a certain number of people in one sequence and then more people in this following one or less people in the following. There are certain people in uniform towards the end who weren't there at the beginning. So we don't know whether it was the same meeting or a different rally. But once again, we can't say who the people are or who the people are declaring themselves as extremists, and we don't know at what point in time the meeting is taking place. Is it prior to the period mentioned in the indictment, after it, during it, or whatever? We have no clue as to that, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Just a comment I would like to make. The Prosecution said there were banners where it says "Jihad." We could see -- he called them flags, but we can see that it is just a white sheet held by two or three individuals and that on it it says "Jihad Brigade," as you yourself, Mr. President, rightly noted a moment ago. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let's continue. And the Prosecution will give us its global response, general -- in general terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the next excerpt is taken from the videotape V0003764. This is an excerpt from the full tape called "Martyrs of Bosnia, Part 1." We have made additional efforts to try and identify the originator, or at least the distributor of this tape. We could make this information available if Your Honour is interested in it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the best thing we can do is to view the excerpt first, and then we'll see later on what we -- what needs clarifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The sequence will be played now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: THE NARRATOR: [In English] Wahiudeen, Mutazu Billah, and Husaamudeen, went to Bosnia to initiate the Jihad efforts there. Wahiudeen met Sheikh Abu Abdul Aziz Azeez [phoen] in Bosnia. Abu Abdul Aziz gave Wahiudeen responsibility for the military operations of the Mujahedin, due to what was known of his ability and experience in this field. He began to think about how to undertake and carry out the Jihad in Bosnia, through an organisation controlled by the Sharia, and by the fact that he was one of those holding a position of responsibility in the Mujahedin Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That was a very brief excerpt in which we could see and hear the commander, Egyptian commander, Wahiudeen, and he was extolling the name of a combatant, a martyr. We saw his photograph, his picture, and we were able to observe that there were certain persons sitting down on benches, and we were wondering whether those are the same benches we saw in the previous sequence. Perhaps the Prosecution will tell us about that. But as we saw people sitting down on benches, we felt we had seen the benches previously. The excerpt was very short. And having said that, Mr. Bourgon, would you like to make any comments?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, the comments I would like to make would be with regard to the additional evidence made by my learned colleague of the Prosecution. We were given the information by the Prosecution this morning concerning the tape itself, and we think that that type of information comes under evidence and that it cannot just be supplied in that way by the Prosecution. If the Prosecution would like to discuss the material they handed over to us this morning, we would have other comments to make. Once again, all I can say is we don't know who the people on the video are, we do not know if the shots of the two people - one with the name Wahiudeen; the other man does not have a name - whether -- where they are. We do indeed see benches, and we are ready to accept that they were the same benches from another sequence, from the previous sequence. But once again, where are we? Who are these people? And what is the date? Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The rest of the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have no comments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Now, the Prosecution has indicated that since yesterday you engaged in some research, and it would appear that within limits, within certain frameworks, you are able to be more specific and give us the specifics about who made the video or any other useful information. So the Defence has just said that it would also like to present its viewpoint, which is quite legitimate and normal. But having said that, would the Prosecution like to tell us anything more, give us some more elements about the videotape?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just a question of clarification. You want to have more elements about the videotape as such or about the potential source, originator, or distributor? I didn't understand correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Defence contests the videotapes founded upon the fact that we don't know the source, we do not know who produced it, et cetera, so anything that you could tell us on that would just help and be of assistance to the Chamber to decide whether they can be tendered into evidence or not. So if you do know any of these elements and can tell us, please do so. The Defence will respond, and then we will weigh up the opinions presented by the two sides and make our own ruling as to admissibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, I will then start with some general remarks and talk, then, briefly about the potential source, originator, or distributor of the last excerpt, the last tape which was shown. Did I understand this order correctly, that you want to proceed in this order? Thank you. Just generally, at this point in time the Prosecution is not in a position to state the exact location. The Prosecution is also not in a position to give the exact date. The Prosecution believes it is a gathering in 1993, probably in August or September 1993. The reason for this is that the commander, Wahiudeen, which is identified or encircled in the last sequence, died subsequently, as Your Honours have heard yesterday in the -- from the -- during the broadcasting of the tape V0003764, one -- the same tape, it was announced that the Commander Wahiudeen died in combat and that his daughter would be five years old, and Your Honours concluded yesterday that this would be about 1998 or that it could be possible that the daughter -- that the video was taken in 1998. What the Prosecution intends to do - we have tried it, but due to the bad quality of the tapes; a first attempt failed - we will make available stills of this flag which has been shown, the flag which shows the Arabic on the upper part and the words "Brigada Jihad" on the lower part. We intend to draw stills from this section, and the Prosecution also intends to draw a still from the scene which was shown on all three tapes where Wahiudeen was sitting or encircled in the last sequence. And the Prosecution intends to ask witnesses who will appear about their knowledge, about either Wahiudeen or the person sitting on the left-hand side of Wahiudeen. It's the Prosecution's position that the person sitting on the left-hand side of Wahiudeen is General Alagic, who was at the time the commander of the OG Bosanska Krajina. With regard to the Defence position that the video could have been taken everywhere in the world, we just heard our translators - I think it was the second sequence - one of the translators translated the word, I think, "extremist" or something from the Bosnian to the English language, so this still doesn't prove that the sequence itself was taken in Bosnia, but it is at least an indication that this didn't happen, let's say, in Afghanistan or any other place in the world. With regard to the potential origin of the third tape, 37 -- V0003764, which was called "The Martyrs of Bosnia, Part 1," the Prosecution would like to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, may we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I turn to the Prosecution. But before giving them the floor to continue with the videotapes, in looking at the general lists, the spreadsheet of all the videos, the Judges have noted that there are videotapes that have not yet been broadcast. So the question is: When do you expect to show them? These are the numbers: 2898, 2414, 2911, 1468, 2629, 2781, 2895, 1676, 3270, 1440, and 1790. So we'd like to know how you intend to proceed. Do you intend to show them? That's my first question. And secondly, when? The best time would be to continue next week, into Monday. As I said, there will be no sittings next week because of the absence of witnesses, so could you inform me of what you intend to do. How far have you come in your thoughts on showing those videotapes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, just one question for clarification: The numbers you have referred to, I -- do I understand this correctly that these are V000-numbers and then the four digits following?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right. The last digits, the figures on the index for the transcripts. I began with 2818, but it says number 6; 2414 is number 7; 2911 is 9; 1468, 11; 2629, 12; and the following are the numbers that followed; 2781, 2898, 1676, 1421, and 1729 -- 22. So I think they're in the binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, Your Honours. With regard to the question you asked, the Prosecution would have at the end of this day announced the decision or would have been prepared not to show these videos, but from your question I understand that Your Honours would like to see excerpts from these videotapes? Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Inasmuch as those videotapes were asked to be introduced into evidence, you asked them to be tendered, so if that is the case - and this was challenged by the Defence; the Chamber gave a ruling saying that we would make our final decision after having seen in open session publicly those videotapes - and there are two main groups, one requiring agreement between the parties - that is to say, we decided not to show them or show them; the others we decided need not be shown - but there is an outstanding number which in the Chamber's opinion should be viewed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is certainly possible, and we are prepared at any point in time to show excerpts -- relevant excerpts from these sequences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Since we have another 40 minutes left approximately, we're going to continue, and we'll continue again on Monday. So we'll be continuing on Monday. Having said that, let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The next video is the last one from Block 3. It is from the videotape V0001737.
