The Prosecution, based on the information about the video -- or from the video itself, is not in a position to give the exact date about this sequence; however, it is a conversation or an interview with two Mujahedin or two males who look like Mujahedin talk about the incorporation of a unit sitting in a tent, and this unit can be the El Mujahed Unit. This sequence is four minutes of duration, running from 0055 minutes 06 until 0059 minutes 05. And since an excerpt from this tape has been shown today already, I cannot -- or I don't need to, I believe, to provide more information about the submitter and so on, since this has already been done. The sequence will be shown now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Brother, what do you think about the Unit Mujahedin? In my opinion, as far as the unit is concerned, God willing, that Allah will take care that this unit survives. However, communism is still in the Bosnian Government, is prevailing, to weaken us, to destroy us. However, God willing, we, the Bosnian people, to fight for the advantages of Islam, we might need time to establish that because we lived with communism for 50 years, and before that we were under Germany, Austro-Hungary, I don't know what else, so it was an unhealthy system to live in. These are all problems that are present in Bosnia and among this people. With other's help, the Bosnian people has come to their senses. With other's help, they started fighting in 1992, and to fight for this unit, the Mujahedin, and that the people are sympathetic towards the unit and that they have started to believe in this unit, in its achievements, as if they knew that every soldier is fighting in the name of Allah, that he is not fighting for this and that, that he is doing that for some-that he is not doing that for some personal benefit. In the name of Allah and the Sharia.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] To believe in Allah, the only creator and in his almightiness, to rely upon him. I would suggest them not to turn to the West and not to rely upon the West, that it's all an illusion, an obvious illusion of their people who have come here and who are giving us minimumhelp. It is obvious that they want to stir up contention among Muslims. I would suggest to them to be on good terms with each other, to look for the cognition, to look for the truth, in order to teach faith to those who do not know it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This excerpt -- about this excerpt, we can say the following: That it -- the scene takes place in a tent, that there are four individuals sitting down who are answering somebody, whom we cannot see a priori. Of those four, three wear battledress. And it is not -- it is with interest that we can note that one of them -- or next to him there is a machine-gun which is resting beside him. In the background - we see this very briefly - that there is a library of some kind with books in it and lots of video cassettes as well, a certain number of video cassettes at any rate. And it is true that all this could be photographed more precisely. Then there's a flag, a banner with an inscription on it in Arabic. The Chamber cannot, of course, translate the inscription on the banner, because it's in Arabic. And there were exchanges between the person asking questions and replying. The soldiers there speak about matters which are either political or military, and we are able to hear at one given point in time one of the soldiers saying that there were problems but that people were beginning to have more sympathy for them. And one can deduce that between the Bosnian-Herzegovinian government and themselves there were problems to address. That was more or less what one could deduce from listening to the soundtrack of the tape and the conversation going on between the individuals speaking. Would the Defence like to comment?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Once again, we don't know who these people are. We do not know where those people are. And especially we don't know what point in time the conversation is taking place. The conversation in itself does not allow us to draw any conclusions, with the absence of a date in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and to draw any other conclusions. Anything that we can say is circumstantial, with respect to the links between the Bosnian government and one of these units. So, Mr. President, once again, we do not see how this exhibit can be used, unless we have a witness come into the courtroom to explain to us who those people are and the general context of the events taking place, the conversation taking place. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Apart from the comments presented by Mr. Bourgon himself, we have nothing to add. No observations from our part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Would the Prosecution like to respond or would you prefer to continue?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution would just add one detail to the summary just given by you. We observed also two hand grenades standing in this -- on the shelf of this library.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I just see my colleague from the Defence on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I think this particular witness testified under protective measures. We can check that out. So may this be stricken from the record if that is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, if the witness did indeed enjoy protective measures, then please have this struck from the record. We will put that right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The person handed the tape over on the 21st of February, 1997 to -- excuse me, this must be an error here. I will submit this information later, but -- at what date it was handed over. But it was handed over to an investigator of the Tribunal, Ms. Racine Manas. The tape has a duration of 37 minutes, and it should be shown in its entirety, which is not possible given the advanced time, but we will stop, with the permission of Your Honour, at quarter to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We could go on perhaps for a few extra minutes. That is feasible, thanks to the obliging interpreters, we can continue for a few minutes beyond the time limit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: One last information for the interpreter. The transcript is contained in tab number 9 of the binder, and we will -- we will show the sequence right now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] Brajkovici, have been present in -- the Croats have been present in these areas since the eleventh century. Before the Muslim-Croatian conflict broke out, exactly 5.700 Croats lived in these areas. They lived in eight villages with 1.128 households. The largest village is Grahovcici, with 276 households; then Cukle, 225 households; Brajkovici, 180 households; the village of Susanj, 158 households; Dolac-Bila, 65; Konjevic, 110; then there is Ovnak, with 58 households; Misonica, with 15; Miletici, 20; then there is the village of Podovi, with 86 households; and the village of Orasac, 35 households. Right in this shot we can see the village of Donje Cukle, the hamlet of Alibasici. Now we can see the hamlet of Softici. This hamlet is inhabited by Bosniaks, Muslims. You can see that the village is intact, it has not suffered any damage. Now, in this shot we can see the Hamlet of Babici, and the house belonging to Franjo Kolenda in the left-hand corner. In the middle, we can see Mirko Babic's house. Then in the lower part of the screen there is the little facility that has been torn down; that's Zeljo Babic's house. Here in this shot we can see Ante Babic's house. Once again, the hamlet of Softici, up above Gornje Cukle, where some 30 Croatian families used to live; the village of Orasac, 35 families lived there before the war. This large facility was built in 1993. It was built by Mujahedin and they used it as a barracks. Until 1994, the village was intact, but when Mujahedin had to leave the village, they destroyed it. No one lives in the village of Orasac at the moment. Another shot showing the village of Orasac in it. Once again, we can see the facility that the Mujahedin of the Muslim unit of El Mujahed used as a barracks. We can see that other houses have been destroyed, demolished. Donje Cukle, the hamlet of Alibasici. Now, this scene shows precisely the houses belonging to Franjo Stojak, Ante Stojak, Jako Stojak, Ilija Stojak and their sons. All the houses were destroyed during the first three days, on the 8th, 9th and 10th of June, 1993. This is the other part of the village where the family name was Jankovic. Drago Jankovic's house, his father Relja's house. This large facility here is the local school, it was also destroyed on the 8th of June,1993. I can't see in whose way that got. Zlatko Tomic's house, in the upper corner. We can see the village chapel, which was built in the 17th century. It meant a lot to these people. Masses used to be held here before establishing--before the Parish Church was built. Once again we can see the village school that was destroyed on the 8th of June,1993. These people have the status of refugees. They mostly live in -- in the towns of Central Bosnia, in Vitez, in Busovaca. Many of them are still in Western Europe, in America and Canada, I mean, in third world countries, in the Republic of Croatia. They intend to come back here. A large number of them have registered to come back. No one lives in the village of Cukle at present, except for several Bosniak families, Muslim families from Western Krajina and Eastern Bosnia. Once again, this is -- we can see nobody but these are the Mrkonja houses, Franjo Mrkonja's house up there. We can see the slopes of Vlasic. Now on the screen we can see the villages of Gornje Maljine and Donje Maljine. Gornje Maljine were inhabited by the Croats. Maljine was burned and demolished on the 8th of June, 1993. In this village, on the slopes of this mountain, the most horrific crime was committed against Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and on June the 8th,1993, 36 Croats were shot there, they were soldiers of the HVO, women and old people. The name of the exact location is Bikose, and their bodies have not been found to this day. Most of the families from Gornje Maljine, Croatian families, have emigrated all over the world. They have the status of refugees in the countries of Western Europe, in the Republic of Croatia, in Slovenia. A number of them live in the towns of Central Bosnia, in Vitez, in Busovaca, in Novi Travnik, and they are going to come back. Once again we can see Bikose. The interesting thing about this parish is that it is situated in the territories of two municipalities. The villages of Konjevici and Susanj are in the municipality of Zenica; whereas, the other villages are in the territory of the Municipality of Travnik. Once again we can see the hamlet of Softici, where Bosniak families, Muslim families live. You see, the village is intact. Not a single house has been destroyed. We are going towards Ovnak. Out there in the distance you can see Ovnak, and the mountain of Lisac is up above. Now in this shot we can see Gornji Brajkovici, the houses belonging to Matija Matkovic and Jozo Matosevic. Behind them is Niko Matosevic's house that was destroyed. There is Ivica Babic's house and the houses of Stipe Kolenda and Vlado Babic. Here we can see Tomo Babic's house, as well as Marinko Suman's and Slavko Miskovic's houses, Novo Naselje, Ovnak, which is a part of the village of Grahovcici. Once again, we can see the village of Cukle, the parish church of Brajkovici, which was built in 1879. The steeple that we can see, or on the steeple is a cross that was torn down on the 8th of June, 1993. The church suffered minor damage, but it was restored last year. What we see right now are the foundations of a burnt-down house, belonging to the late Ante Klaric, an old man in his seventies, who did not want to leave his home as the Muslim forces attacked this parish. He stayed at home, and unfortunately he was killed. These are the foundations of the stable. Once again we can see the foundation of the house. The body of the late Ante Klaric was found a month after he had been killed, in a well, in front of a house belonging to his cousin Stipe Klaric. Later on we are going to give you a shot of that well too. Ante was buried in the local graveyard, which is called Bogus [phoen]. These are the houses belonging to Ante's cousins. Now we can see the house of his younger cousin, whose name is Ante Klaric, then the houses of Stipe Klaric, Mate Klaric. This restored house belongs to Ante's cousin Drago Klaric. It was restored several days ago by a Dutch donation organisation El Soldateris. You see, it's all been destroyed, demolished. It all happened in a day. Once again we can see the parish church. There we cannot see the cross on the steeple. The village of Brajkovici; Zarko Viskovic's house; the house belonging to Zarko's brother Marjan, to his brother Nenad, to their sister Kata. It has also been burned. Once again, a shot showing the Viskovic brothers' house; Mate Klaric's house here. We can see the well that Anto Klaric's body was found in in front of his cousin Stipe's house. Drago Klaric's house. And deeper in there you can see the village of Grahovcici. We are going towards Ovnak. Gornji Brajkovici, the houses belonging to Ivica Babic, Vlado Babic, and Pero Babic. Now we can see the house of Niko Matosevic, which was demolished and burnt, but about a month ago it was blown up. This was reported to Travnik MUP, but the perpetrators have not yet been found. This is one of many cases of a repeated devastation and destruction of houses. Vlado Babic's house, Frano Matosevic's house, Bozo Tustonja's house, and Zarko Radic's house, Zarko's brother house, and his cousin Ante Radic's house. Then we have Stipe Bilic's house, which he built for his son, Nikola. Unfortunately, Nikola was killed. Zvonko Kolenda's house, which he built a year or two before the war. You see, it's been demolished and looted. In the background are the houses belonging to the Barac brothers, Niko, Vinko and Frano. Tomo Babic's house, where a shop used to be. Here we can see once again Marinko Suman's house, where the Trenk cafe and bar used to be located, the place where young people gathered, and there was also a local supermarket. The house was looted and demolished. Slavko Miskovic's house, it was built one year before this terrible war. You see, the house has been looted and demolished. In the background, we see the houses belonging to Ivica Kolenda, Marko Pesa, Matija Kafadar, Ivica Pesa, Stanko, sons Niko, Bozo. the house belonging to Ivica Kafadar and his son Mirko, also known as Dzilda. Nikola Kafadar's house; you see, there it reads: "7th Muslim Brigade". Houses belonging to Nevenka Miskovic, Ivo Vuleta. The local cemetery of Ovnak. This is where they buried the old people from the village of Susanj who had been killed. Right here 18 old people from the village of Susanj were brought here and killed on the 8th of June, 1993. Reportedly they were supposed to be soldiers of the HVO. They were elderly people between the ages of 65 and 80, and their last names were mostly Markovic and Vidosevic. In the background you can see the village of Susanj. We are entering the new part of the village of Grahovcici, a new settlement. Marijan Radic's house, the house belonging to Ante Babic and his brother Jozo, the house belonging to Drago Radic and his brother Fabo; Zivko Barbic's house; Stipe Jandric's house; the house belonging to the Jandric brothers, Zvonko, Tomo, Franjo and Drago - Dragan; a recently restored house belonging to Fabijan Dzaip. Also, recently restored house of Franjo Filipovic, also known as Foltin. Now we are moving towards the central part of the village of Grahovcici. On the screen we can see the picture of Pero Filipovic, Anto Matosevic and Anto's sons. The houses have no roofs; they have been burned and looted. As I said, the village of Grahovcici is the largest village in the parish of Brajkovici and the largest village in the Travnik municipality. In this shot, we can see the hamlet of Radici and the houses of Vinko Radic, Jozo Radic, Marko Cuturic. In the background are the houses of the Musanic family, the house belonging to Tomo Perkic and his brother, Sarafin Perkic; Anto Matosevic's house, Ante's father's house, Drago, it has been demolished and burnt. Once again, we can see Marko Cuturic's house, Franjo Cuturic's house. Now we can see the local cemetery of Svib. Most of the gravestones have been destroyed. They were destroyed in 1993, in 1994, and even in 1995 cases of demolishing tombstones were registered. We are moving towards the centre of the village. The house with the red roof is Tomo Cuturic's house. It was restored recently. In the background you can see the Grahovcici open cast mine. Then, there are the houses of Jozo Cuturic, Luko Jadrinic, Luko's son Franjo, and again the open cast mine in the background. Right next to the open cast mine, an underground mine was opened, a shaft mine for excavating coal, and as a result the village is being undermined. That is a huge problem for the people from the village. Massive landslides and tectonic disturbances were been caused, and when the time comes there are slim chances that they are going to be able to build anything in this village. Somebody has been doing it deliberately and is still doing it. People tried to stop this excavation any way they could, but it is difficult to solve this problem. In this shot, we can see the houses belonging to Tomo Cuturic, Sreco Cuturic, his brother Ante, the houses belonging to Tomo Cuturic and another man with the same name, to Drago Cuturic, Vito Palavra; the houses belonging to Ante Cuturic and Ivica. this part of the village was mostly inhabited by people whose last name is Cuturic. They were close relatives. We can see the local school, which was built in and was also burned on the 8th of June, 1993. Once again, we can see the house of Ante Matko, Ante Cuturic, also known as Antic. These red roofs, the hamlet of Barbici. These houses were restored a short while ago, and the repair work is still in progress. The work is being done by the donation organisation El Soldateris. The Dutch and French governments are the ones who provided donations to restore these houses. The house belonging to Tomo Barbic, Zarko, Silva. That's what we see. Here you can see the local cemetery of Vinisce, one of the oldest cemeteries, oldest Catholic cemeteries in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Now we can see most of the parish territory. Once again, the Parish Church of St. Peter and St. Paul in Brajkovici. Brajkovici and Susanj are the only villages in the Parish that have not been vandalised. Grahovcici fared worst; all the houses were destroyed. The extent of destruction of each house is 80 to 100 per cent. Once again, the local cemetery of Vinisce, where there is a Bogumil tombstone from -- dating back to 1011, and the village was named after it later on. It was named after Mihovil Grahovcic, who was buried in this cemetery. Drago Sikalo's house. Now we can see Pero Jandric's house, and beyond there is the hamlet of Babici. You see, everything has been demolished. The house with the red roof has been restored recently by the Dutch government; as well as this second one and the third one. The entrance to the village of Grahovcici, the hamlet of Milika and the house belonging to the Filipovic family. Then we come to the hamlet of Ovnak and the house belonging to the Jandric brothers and the Radic brothers. Now we can see from a different angle again the hamlet of Otici and the houses belonging to the Bilic brothers, Slavko, Karlo and Ante. All families with the second name Bilic lived here; the houses belonging to Drago Bilic, then Zorko Bilic, Vesko Bilic, Ante Bilic; they are brothers. The house belonging to their cousin Stipe Bilic, Stipe's son Nikola. Once again, from a different angle, the houses belonging to Drago Bilic, Zorko, Ante. The houses belonging to Vesko Bilic, Fabo Jandric. On the hill we can see a house, a house again, and it belongs to Vesko Bilic, and another shot of the house belong to Drago and Zorko Bilic, from a different angle this time. The same image from a different angle. Restoring is going to take a lot of funds. It all has to be built from the foundations upwards. Here we see Stipe Bilic's house and in the background his son's house, Pavo. The large house belonging to Niko Bilic and his son. One of the oldest cemeteries, Catholic cemeteries in Bosnia and Herzegovina, we can see the chapel that was destroyed and demolished. These Bogumil tombstones date back from the tenth and the eleventh centuries. Most of the tombstones have been destroyed, not only in the cemetery of Vinisce but also in the Sviba cemetery and the Sikalo cemetery, in all the cemeteries, in fact, in the Parish of Brajkovici. 80 per cent of the tombstones have been destroyed. The only cemetery that remained intact is the Ovnak cemetery, which passes right next to the Travnik-Zenica road. Now we can see the gravestone of the Pavlovic family, you can see when she was buried, when she died, in 1966. I can't see how she could possibly have been in the way of those who destroyed it. See Pero Barbic, buried in 1976, and the same thing applies to him. Once again, their gravestones have been demolished, a cross broken. The same thing happened to this gravestone. This is the gravestone of the Barbic family. It says, "Mijo Barbic, killed -- or rather died in 1962. Veronika Barbic, died in 1963." As I have already said, this same situation is with the cemeteries in the parish of Brajkovici, and as I've said, the shaft mine for coal excavation in the village of Grahovcici. Behind the open cast mine the mining infrastructure stands. This shaft mine was opened with the sole purpose of causing tectonic disturbances there and to prevent the people from returning. The Croats in this region call it a "political coal mine". A lot has been done to stop this, but there is someone more powerful behind this project. Another shot of the central part of the village. In the background we see the hamlet of Radici. Stipe Sikalo's house, also destroyed; it was burnt on the 8th of June, 1993. Vito Palavra's house. We are repeating the same shot, the central part of the village, mostly the houses of the families with the same surname, the surname of Cuturic, Sreco, Tomo, Ante. All these people have registered to come back here and they are certainly going to return. However, the problem now is to solve the problem with the coal mine in Grahovcici. That has to be dealt with. This is the local school. I hope that children will attend their classes here again. Perhaps as early as the next year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to have to end there. Just a very quick sentence before we adjourn. The tape is of excellent quality. It was made in winter with sunlight, which allows us to see the whole very well. The general scene is a desolate landscape. All the villages are mentioned by the commentator. Their names are mentioned; Ovnak, Susanj, Grahovcici, Cukle, Maljine, and so on. And the narrator identifies the houses one by one and gives us the names of the owners. It appears that several houses but very few have been restored; otherwise, all the rest are in a state of destruction and demolition on the -- there are no people in the videotape, and the feeling one gets in viewing this videotape is that all the villagers have left, because you can't see a single person. There's some -- one element furnished by one of the witnesses. He said that when you are up on one hill, you can see all the other hills, which means that the person filming, thanks to the zoom lens, can zoom in on the different villages, and they are five to ten kilometres, at a distance between each other of five to ten kilometres. As far as the Judges can see, it is a village with a Mujahedin barracks that we see on the screen. And as the commentator said, it was abandoned or destroyed, but we can actually see a building of several storeys which sort of sticks out from the general landscape where there are no other similar constructions, houses constructed that way. And certain houses were under recent construction. There were destroyed and damaged churches as well and cemeteries where the tombstones and crosses were destroyed. So that is a very brief overview of what the -- we saw on the videotapes and what will be recorded on the transcript. I'm afraid we can't go on. It's already 2.00. On Monday I will be giving the floor to the Defence counsel, and they'll have the whole weekend to prepare their observations and comments for us on Monday. So we reconvene on Monday when we shall see the remaining tapes played to us by the Prosecution. And I'm sure we're going to finish those on Monday. As I said, we won't be sitting on Tuesday; we will be sitting on Wednesday; and I don't think we'll be sitting either on Thursday or Friday, but we'll reconvene on the following Monday. I apologise to the staff for asking them to stay on, but we wish to complete this -- these documents and to express what we've seen. The meeting is adjourned until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 7th day of June, 2004, at 2.15 p.m.
